chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan from his father from Abu Jamilah from Muhammad ibn Marwan from al-Fudayl ibn Yasar, who said:

Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: In the case of a man who died and left behind his wife and his 'asabah (male agnates), and left one thousand dirhams. His wife presented evidence for five hundred dirhams, so she took it and took her inheritance. Then a man claimed against him one thousand dirhams, and he had no evidence, so the woman confessed to him. Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'She confessed to the loss of one-third of her property, and she has no inheritance. The woman takes two-thirds of the five hundred, and returns to him what remains, because her confession against herself is like evidence.'

key_terms.بِمَنْزِلَةِ: In the status of / equivalent to

ai.seo_question: How does a wife's confession to an unproven debt affect her inheritance share in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) establishes that a wife’s voluntary confession to an unproven debt is treated with the same evidentiary weight as formal proof, leading to the forfeiture of her inheritance share. This ruling highlights the Shia legal principle that a confession (iqrar) against one's own interest in matters of estate distribution is binding, ensuring creditors are prioritized over heirs when the estate is insufficient. The scenario illustrates the delicate balance between preserving the rights of creditors and the entitlements of heirs in posthumous financial settlements.
